clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive transgredient palmoplantar keratoderma originally described on the Adriatic island of Mljet (Meleda)
Caused by biallelic variants in SLURP1, which encodes a secreted lymphocyte antigen-6 protein modulating cholinergic signalling and keratinocyte differentiation
The keratoderma extends beyond the palms and soles onto the dorsa of the hands and feet (the transgredient pattern), often with a well-demarcated erythematous border
Progressive constricting bands (pseudo-ainhum) can develop around digits and may lead to autoamputation
Associated features include hyperhidrosis with malodour, secondary fungal and bacterial infection, nail changes and perioral erythema
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by the family history and SLURP1 molecular testing
Management is supportive with keratolytics, emollients, oral retinoids in severe disease, meticulous foot care and treatment of secondary infection
reference.pathophysiology: Mal de Meleda is caused by loss-of-function variants in SLURP1, encoding secreted Ly-6/uPAR-related protein 1, which acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors to regulate keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis and to modulate skin inflammation. Deficiency disturbs the balance of epidermal proliferation and terminal differentiation in acral skin, producing a thick, diffuse transgredient keratoderma. Accompanying hyperhidrosis and barrier disruption predispose to maceration, malodour and secondary infection, while chronic inflammation and fibrous constriction can create pseudo-ainhum.
additionalDifferentials: Other diffuse hereditary palmoplantar keratodermas (e.g. Vörner/Unna-Thost)
Acquired keratoderma from inflammatory or infective causes
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing orthohyperkeratosis with acanthosis
Mycological and bacterial swabs for secondary infection
Clinical examination for pseudo-ainhum and digital constriction
redFlags: Constricting fibrous bands (pseudo-ainhum) risking digital autoamputation
Deep secondary infection or cellulitis of macerated acral skin
Rapidly progressive or asymmetrical thickening raising concern for malignant change
Severe functional impairment of hands or feet
reference.prognosis: The keratoderma is lifelong and tends to progress through childhood; with diligent skin and foot care most patients maintain function, but pseudo-ainhum, recurrent infection and disability can complicate severe cases.
pitfalls: Missing the transgredient spread onto dorsal skin that distinguishes it from common diffuse keratodermas
Overlooking early pseudo-ainhum that is amenable to intervention before autoamputation
Failing to treat the secondary fungal and bacterial colonisation that worsens odour and maceration
Not offering genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder
management: Regular application of keratolytic emollients such as urea, salicylic acid or lactic acid preparations to soften and reduce the transgredient keratoderma
Topical or, for severe disease, systemic retinoids such as acitretin to reduce hyperkeratosis, with monitoring for mucocutaneous and skeletal adverse effects
Mechanical paring and debridement of thickened palmoplantar skin with podiatry input to preserve function and mobility
Control of hyperhidrosis and malodour with antiperspirants, absorbent measures and topical botulinum toxin where troublesome
Prompt treatment of secondary bacterial and fungal infection with appropriate antimicrobials guided by mycological and bacterial swabs
Regular surveillance for constricting digital bands (pseudo-ainhum) with early surgical release to prevent autoamputation
Autosomal recessive inheritance warrants genetic counselling and SLURP1 testing for at-risk family members
